entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with plant or seaweed material. The useful colour, gum, wax or other component is separated from the raw material, then concentrated, refined or purified for food use.
entries.tile_summary: A red-purple plant pigment associated with alkanet root.
entries.expanded_summary: A red-purple plant pigment associated with alkanet root. Alkannin is the principal colouring substance found in the root of plants in the borage family.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Obtained from alkanet plant material by extraction and purification of its red colouring compounds.
entries.fact_1_copy: Alkannin occurs in the root bark of alkanet plants.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used as a colour where permitted.

entries.tile_summary: Erythrosine is a bright pink-red synthetic dye in the xanthene family.
entries.expanded_summary: Erythrosine is a bright pink-red synthetic dye in the xanthene family. Its colour comes from an iodine-containing form of fluorescein.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by chemical synthesis, including iodination of a fluorescein-based colour molecule.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used when a vivid pink to cherry-red colour is wanted.
entries.fact_2_copy: It is an iodinated colour compound, not a source of dietary iodine in the ordinary nutritional sense.

entries.tile_summary: Fast Green FCF is a synthetic green food colour made to deliver a strong, consistent green shade.
entries.expanded_summary: Fast Green FCF is a synthetic green food colour made to deliver a strong, consistent green shade.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by chemical synthesis and purified to food-additive specifications.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used to add or restore green colour.

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with an existing material — natural or manufactured — and deliberately transforms it using processes such as heating, roasting, oxidation, hydrolysis, neutralisation or other controlled treatment. The starting material can be materially changed in colour, structure or food-technology behaviour.
entries.tile_summary: Vegetable carbon is an intensely black colouring made from carbon-rich plant material.
entries.expanded_summary: Vegetable carbon is an intensely black colouring made from carbon-rich plant material. The material is carbonised and purified rather than used as ordinary charcoal.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by controlled carbonisation of vegetable material followed by purification and fine processing.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used for black or very dark colouring.
entries.fact_2_copy: The carbon can originate from plant material even though the final ingredient is predominantly elemental carbon.
entries.evidence_copy: Europe's earlier assessment found no safety concern at reported uses provided residues of potentially cancer-causing combustion chemicals were tightly limited. In 2026, the authority confirmed that commercial 153 can contain many very small particles, including nanoparticles, but said the submitted particle information was not sufficient to complete a nanoscale assessment. This is a defined gap about particle behaviour and specifications; it is not evidence that eating 153 has been shown to cause harm.
entries.evidence_source_1_link_label: European food-safety authority: Amendment of the specifications for vegetable carbon E153 (2026)

entries.tile_summary: A yellow-orange carotenoid-type colour related to naturally occurring carotenoids.
entries.expanded_summary: beta-apo-8′-Carotenal is a carotenoid-type yellow-orange colour structurally related to naturally occurring carotenoids, but food-grade material is manufactured as a defined colour ingredient.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by controlled chemical synthesis and formulated to protect the colour from oxidation.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used for yellow to orange colouring.
entries.fact_2_copy: Its molecular family is the same broad pigment family that includes beta-carotene.

entries.source_profile_definition: The same additive identity can legitimately be made from different starting materials or by different manufacturing routes. The additive code alone therefore cannot tell you one reliable origin.
entries.tile_summary: Violoxanthin is a carotenoid-family pigment associated with yellow colouring.
entries.expanded_summary: Violoxanthin is a carotenoid-family pigment associated with yellow colouring. It belongs to the same broad natural pigment family as beta-carotene and lutein.
entries.source_preparation_copy: This carotenoid occurs in natural biological sources; commercial food-colour preparations may depend on the approved source and manufacturing specification.
entries.fact_1_copy: A xanthophyll carotenoid.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used for yellow colouring where permitted.

entries.tile_summary: Mineral-like iron oxide pigments that range from yellow and red to black depending on the oxide form.
entries.expanded_summary: Mineral-like iron oxide pigments that range from yellow and red to black depending on the oxide form.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced from purified mineral material or by controlled manufacture of defined iron oxides.
entries.fact_1_copy: Different iron oxide forms produce yellow, red, brown or black shades.
entries.fact_2_copy: These are inorganic iron-oxygen compounds.

entries.tile_summary: Sodium sorbate is the sodium salt of sorbic acid.
entries.expanded_summary: Sodium sorbate is the sodium salt of sorbic acid. It is used in food mainly for preservation rather than for flavour.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Made by neutralising sorbic acid with a sodium source, producing a more water-soluble sorbate salt.
entries.fact_1_copy: One of the sorbate preservatives.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used to inhibit moulds and yeasts.

entries.expanded_summary: Calcium benzoate is the calcium salt of benzoic acid. It is used in food mainly for preservation rather than for flavour.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Made by reacting benzoic acid with a calcium source.
entries.fact_1_copy: One of the benzoate preservatives.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used to slow microbial spoilage in suitable foods.

entries.source_profile_definition: Includes minerals and simple salts, acids, bases, oxides and related compounds. Some are refined directly from mineral deposits; others are made by reacting basic mineral-derived or industrial starting materials and then purified.
entries.tile_summary: Code 223 identifies sodium metabisulphite, a sulphite preservative. That's particularly useful to know for people who are sensitive to sulphites.
entries.expanded_summary: Sodium metabisulphite (223) belongs to the sulphite preservative family. When dissolved, it can provide preservative and anti-browning action through sulphite-related compounds.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Manufactured from sulphur dioxide and sodium alkali, then crystallised as the metabisulphite salt.
entries.fact_1_copy: Part of the sulphite preservative family.
entries.fact_2_copy: A solid ingredient that can provide sulphur dioxide preservative action in food.
entries.evidence_copy: For safety purposes, authorities assess 223 together with the other sulphites. Recent European modelling found the smallest safety margins in high consumers, especially where diets contained more dried fruit, drinks or preserved foods. Australia and New Zealand's food regulator considers a general risk at current food levels unlikely, but labels must declare added sulphites from 10 milligrams per kilogram. For a sulphite-sensitive person, 223 is therefore an actionable label signal.

entries.evidence_source_2_link_label: European food-safety authority: Update of dietary exposure to sulphur dioxide-sulphites E220-228 (2025)

entries.tile_summary: Ethyl lauroyl arginate is an antimicrobial compound built from lauric acid, the amino acid arginine and ethanol.
entries.expanded_summary: Ethyl lauroyl arginate is an antimicrobial compound built from lauric acid, the amino acid arginine and ethanol. It is designed to disrupt microbial cell membranes.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Manufactured through controlled chemical reactions that join lauric-acid and arginine-derived components, followed by purification.
entries.fact_1_copy: Includes a fatty-acid component and an amino-acid-derived component.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used as an antimicrobial preservative in specified foods and drinks.

entries.tile_summary: Sodium acetate or sodium diacetate is an acetate salt derived from acetic acid.
entries.expanded_summary: Sodium acetate or sodium diacetate is an acetate salt derived from acetic acid. It provides acetate chemistry without adding acetic acid in exactly the same form.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Made by neutralising acetic acid with a sodium-containing base; diacetate forms also contain associated acetic acid.
entries.fact_1_copy: Chemically related to the acid found in vinegar.
entries.fact_2_copy: Depending on the salt and food, can help regulate acidity, preserve or influence flavour.

entries.tile_summary: Calcium propionate is the calcium salt of propionic acid.
entries.expanded_summary: Calcium propionate is the calcium salt of propionic acid. It is used mainly as a mould-inhibiting preservative.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Made by neutralising propionic acid with a calcium-containing base and purifying the resulting salt.
entries.fact_1_copy: Commonly associated with preservation of bread and other bakery products.
entries.fact_2_copy: Releases propionate, the active acid-related preserving species, under food conditions.

The liquid or culture is then filtered or separated, and the additive is concentrated and purified. The finished additive normally does not contain live production microbes.
entries.tile_summary: Sodium ascorbate is the sodium salt of ascorbic acid — vitamin C.
entries.expanded_summary: Sodium ascorbate is the sodium salt of ascorbic acid — vitamin C. It provides ascorbate antioxidant chemistry in a salt form.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Made by neutralising purified ascorbic acid with a sodium-containing base; the ascorbic acid itself is usually produced from glucose by industrial fermentation/chemical processing.
entries.fact_1_copy: It is chemically related to vitamin C and supplies ascorbate.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used mainly for antioxidant, colour-protection or processing effects.

entries.tile_summary: dl-Alpha-tocopherol is a synthetic form of alpha-tocopherol, the vitamin-E molecule.
entries.expanded_summary: dl-Alpha-tocopherol is a synthetic form of alpha-tocopherol, the vitamin-E molecule. It is a mixture of stereoisomers rather than the single natural stereoisomer found in foods.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by chemical synthesis from smaller precursor molecules and purified.
entries.fact_1_copy: It belongs to the vitamin E family.
entries.fact_2_copy: The 'dl-' designation distinguishes the synthetic stereoisomer mixture from naturally sourced d-alpha-tocopherol.

entries.tile_summary: Erythorbic acid is a stereoisomer of ascorbic acid — chemically very similar to vitamin C but arranged differently in space.
entries.expanded_summary: Erythorbic acid is a stereoisomer of ascorbic acid — chemically very similar to vitamin C but arranged differently in space. It is used mainly for antioxidant and colour-stabilising effects rather than as a vitamin source.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced industrially from carbohydrate starting materials through controlled chemical and/or fermentation steps, then purified.
entries.fact_1_copy: It closely resembles ascorbic acid chemically but does not have the same vitamin activity.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used as an antioxidant and in cured-food colour chemistry.

entries.expanded_summary: Sodium lactate is the sodium salt of lactic acid. It keeps the familiar lactic-acid chemistry but in a less acidic salt form.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Made by neutralising lactic acid — commonly produced by fermentation of sugars — with a sodium-containing base.
entries.fact_1_copy: Derived from lactic acid, the acid associated with many fermented foods.
entries.fact_2_copy: Depending on the salt, can regulate acidity, retain moisture, firm texture or support preservation.

entries.expanded_summary: Sodium citrate / sodium dihydrogen citrate is a sodium salt of citric acid. It is used when food technologists want citrate chemistry with less direct acidity than citric acid itself.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Made by neutralising fermentation-produced citric acid with a sodium-containing base and crystallising the salt.
entries.fact_1_copy: Derived from citric acid, the acid naturally associated with citrus fruit.
entries.fact_2_copy: Commonly used to regulate acidity, buffer pH or provide mineral/citrate functionality.

entries.expanded_summary: Potassium sodium tartrate is a potassium and sodium salt of tartaric acid, the fruit acid closely associated with grapes and wine.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by neutralising purified tartaric acid or recovering and refining naturally formed tartrate salts from food-processing streams.
entries.fact_1_copy: Built from tartaric acid chemistry.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used for acidity control, buffering, stabilisation or raising-agent chemistry depending on the salt.

entries.expanded_summary: Magnesium phosphates are a family of magnesium salts of phosphoric acid. Schedule 8 groups several mono-, di- or tribasic forms under the same additive number.

entries.fact_1_copy: Different phosphate forms have different acidity, solubility and buffering behaviour.
entries.fact_2_copy: Depending on the form, phosphates can regulate acidity, act in raising systems, stabilise texture or bind water.

entries.expanded_summary: Rosemary extract is an antioxidant-rich extract from rosemary leaves. The food additive is standardised for compounds such as carnosic acid and carnosol rather than being ordinary dried rosemary herb.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by extracting rosemary leaves, removing much of the flavour/aroma material and concentrating the antioxidant components.
entries.fact_1_copy: Derived from Rosmarinus officinalis / Salvia rosmarinus leaves.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used to slow oxidation, especially in fats and oils.
entries.fact_3_copy: Its purpose is antioxidant protection; it need not make the food taste strongly of rosemary.

entries.tile_summary: Propylene glycol alginate is a chemically modified form of seaweed-derived alginic acid.
entries.expanded_summary: Propylene glycol alginate is a chemically modified form of seaweed-derived alginic acid. Adding propylene glycol ester groups changes how the alginate behaves in acidic foods and emulsions.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Starts with alginic acid from brown seaweed, then undergoes controlled esterification with propylene oxide/propylene glycol chemistry.
entries.fact_1_copy: Seaweed-derived alginate.
entries.fact_2_copy: The modification improves solubility and stability in conditions where ordinary alginate may behave differently.

entries.expanded_summary: Guar gum is a galactomannan extracted from the endosperm of guar seeds. It is a plant-derived hydrocolloid used to manage texture and water in foods.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Collected or extracted from guar beans, then cleaned, milled and/or purified to food-grade specifications.
entries.fact_1_copy: A high-molecular-weight carbohydrate rather than a simple sugar.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used for thickening, stabilising or controlling texture.

entries.tile_summary: Gellan gum is a gel-forming carbohydrate produced by bacterial fermentation.
entries.expanded_summary: Gellan gum is a gel-forming carbohydrate produced by bacterial fermentation. Small amounts can create anything from soft fluid gels to firm, clear gels depending on minerals and formulation.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by fermenting carbohydrate with Sphingomonas bacteria, then recovering and purifying the gellan polymer.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used to gel, stabilise and suspend particles.
entries.fact_2_copy: Its behaviour can be tuned by mineral ions and by the type of gellan preparation.

entries.tile_summary: Polysorbate 80 is an emulsifier made from sorbitol-derived material, polyoxyethylene chains and oleic acid.
entries.expanded_summary: Polysorbate 80 is an emulsifier made from sorbitol-derived material, polyoxyethylene chains and oleic acid. Its molecular design gives it both water-friendly and fat-friendly parts.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by esterifying sorbitol/sorbitan with fatty acids and adding polyoxyethylene chains through controlled chemical processing.
entries.fact_1_copy: Helps oils, fats and water stay mixed and can stabilise foams or dispersions.
entries.fact_2_copy: The fatty-acid feedstock may come from plant or animal fats, while the final emulsifier is chemically processed.
entries.evidence_copy: Europe's food-safety authority assessed polysorbates as a group. It found very low short-term toxicity and no evidence of gene damage, cancer or harm to development, then set a group daily safety limit of 25 milligrams per kilogram of body weight. Its highest estimated exposure for toddlers was 24.5 milligrams per kilogram, very close to that limit, and some food categories lacked use data. This is a defined high-exposure margin for polysorbates, not evidence that all emulsifiers behave alike.
entries.evidence_source_1_link_label: European food-safety authority: Re-evaluation of polysorbates E432-436 (2015)

entries.fact_2_copy: Used particularly to help flavour oils remain evenly dispersed in beverages.

entries.expanded_summary: Microcrystalline and powdered cellulose are purified forms of cellulose, the structural fibre that makes up plant cell walls. They are not digestible like ordinary starch.

entries.expanded_summary: Fatty acid salts are soap-like salts made from food fatty acids and metals such as sodium, potassium, calcium or magnesium. The same broad fatty-acid building blocks occur naturally in fats and oils.

entries.fact_2_copy: Used as anticaking agents, emulsifiers, glazing aids or processing agents depending on the salt.

entries.fact_2_copy: Used as emulsifiers and texture/process aids, with some forms particularly important in bakery applications.

entries.fact_1_copy: Used only in specific technological applications where copper chemistry is required.

entries.source_profile_definition: Includes minerals and simple salts, acids, bases, oxides and related compounds. Some are refined directly from mineral deposits; others are made by reacting basic mineral-derived or industrial starting materials and then purified.
entries.tile_summary: Sodium ferrocyanide is an inorganic complex salt used mainly as an anticaking agent.
entries.expanded_summary: Sodium ferrocyanide is an inorganic complex salt used mainly as an anticaking agent. Despite the word 'cyanide' in the chemical name, the cyanide groups are tightly bound within a stable iron-cyanide complex rather than present as free cyanide.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by forming and crystallising a controlled ferrocyanide complex with sodium ions.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used at low levels to keep salt and other powders free-flowing.
entries.fact_2_copy: The compound is chemically distinct from free hydrogen cyanide or simple cyanide salts.

entries.source_profile_definition: Includes minerals and simple salts, acids, bases, oxides and related compounds. Some are refined directly from mineral deposits; others are made by reacting basic mineral-derived or industrial starting materials and then purified.
entries.tile_summary: Magnesium silicate / talc is magnesium-silicate minerals or manufactured magnesium silicate.
entries.expanded_summary: Magnesium silicate / talc is magnesium-silicate minerals or manufactured magnesium silicate.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Obtained from purified talc mineral or produced by precipitation depending on the form.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used as an anticaking, glazing or processing material.

entries.source_profile_definition: Includes minerals and simple salts, acids, bases, oxides and related compounds. Some are refined directly from mineral deposits; others are made by reacting basic mineral-derived or industrial starting materials and then purified.
entries.tile_summary: Potassium silicate is a soluble alkaline potassium silicate.
entries.expanded_summary: Potassium silicate is a soluble alkaline potassium silicate.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by reacting silica with potassium carbonate or potassium hydroxide at high temperature or in solution.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used for specialised processing and surface-treatment functions.

entries.source_profile_definition: Microorganisms such as bacteria, yeasts or fungi are grown in controlled tanks and fed sugars or other nutrients. They make the target substance as they grow. The liquid or culture is then filtered or separated, and the additive is concentrated and purified. The finished additive normally does not contain live production microbes.
entries.tile_summary: Ferrous gluconate is the iron salt of gluconic acid, an acid made by oxidising glucose.
entries.expanded_summary: Ferrous gluconate is the iron salt of gluconic acid, an acid made by oxidising glucose. The gluconate part is highly water-compatible and can bind minerals.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced from fermentation/oxidation-derived gluconic acid followed by neutralisation with a iron-containing source.
entries.fact_1_copy: Glucose-derived gluconic acid.
entries.fact_2_copy: Depending on the mineral, used for mineral delivery, acidity control, sequestration, colour stabilisation or processing.

entries.source_profile_definition: Microorganisms such as bacteria, yeasts or fungi are grown in controlled tanks and fed sugars or other nutrients. They make the target substance as they grow. The liquid or culture is then filtered or separated, and the additive is concentrated and purified. The finished additive normally does not contain live production microbes.
entries.tile_summary: Calcium glutamate is the calcium salt of glutamic acid, the amino acid associated with umami taste.
entries.expanded_summary: Calcium glutamate is the calcium salt of glutamic acid, the amino acid associated with umami taste. It belongs to the same glutamate flavour-enhancer family as MSG.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Glutamic acid is commonly produced by microbial fermentation of sugars or starch hydrolysates, then neutralised with a calcium source to make the salt.
entries.fact_1_copy: Glutamate occurs naturally in foods including tomatoes, mushrooms, seaweed and aged cheeses.
entries.fact_2_copy: The glutamate ion provides savoury umami taste.
entries.fact_3_copy: Added glutamate and naturally occurring glutamate are the same glutamate ion once dissolved in food.

entries.source_profile_definition: Built from simpler starting chemicals through one or more controlled chemical reactions, then separated and purified to a defined food-grade composition. The starting chemicals may themselves come from petroleum, minerals, plants or other industrial sources; the substance-specific description should say when a notable origin is known.
entries.tile_summary: Maltol is a sweet-smelling flavour-enhancing compound with caramel-like and toasted notes.
entries.expanded_summary: Maltol is a sweet-smelling flavour-enhancing compound with caramel-like and toasted notes. It occurs naturally in some roasted foods and plant materials, but commercial food-grade maltol is generally manufactured.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Usually produced by chemical synthesis and purified as a defined flavour-enhancing compound.
entries.fact_1_copy: Can strengthen sweet, caramel, baked or roasted flavour impressions.
entries.fact_2_copy: Maltol can form naturally during heating and occurs in some plants and foods.
entries.fact_3_copy: Used as a flavour enhancer rather than as a bulk sweetener.

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with plant or seaweed material. The useful colour, gum, wax or other component is separated from the raw material, then concentrated, refined or purified for food use.
entries.tile_summary: Carnauba wax is a hard plant wax collected from the leaves of the Brazilian carnauba palm.
entries.expanded_summary: Carnauba wax is a hard plant wax collected from the leaves of the Brazilian carnauba palm. It is one of the hardest natural waxes used in food.
entries.source_preparation_copy: The dried palm leaves are beaten or brushed to release wax, which is then melted, filtered and refined.
entries.fact_1_copy: Leaves of Copernicia prunifera, the carnauba palm.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used for glossy protective coatings on confectionery, fruit and other foods.

entries.source_profile_definition: A purified gas used in or around food. It may dissolve into the product, displace oxygen in a package, create bubbles or foam, or act as a propellant.
entries.tile_summary: Nitrous oxide is a gas composed of nitrogen and oxygen, best known in food for pressurising and aerating whipped cream.
entries.expanded_summary: Nitrous oxide is a gas composed of nitrogen and oxygen, best known in food for pressurising and aerating whipped cream.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced industrially from controlled decomposition of ammonium nitrate and highly purified.
entries.fact_1_copy: Dissolves well in fat, which makes it useful for creating stable whipped-cream foams as well as acting as a propellant.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used for its gas/pressure properties rather than as a conventional solid or liquid ingredient.

entries.consumer_display_name: Cyclamate or calcium cyclamate or sodium cyclamate
entries.entry_title: Cyclamate or calcium cyclamate or sodium cyclamate (952)
entries.source_profile_definition: Built from simpler starting chemicals through one or more controlled chemical reactions, then separated and purified to a defined food-grade composition. The starting chemicals may themselves come from petroleum, minerals, plants or other industrial sources; the substance-specific description should say when a notable origin is known.
entries.tile_summary: Cyclamates are high-intensity sweeteners based on cyclamic acid; Schedule 8 includes the parent acid and its sodium and calcium salts.
entries.expanded_summary: Cyclamates are high-intensity sweeteners based on cyclamic acid; Schedule 8 includes the parent acid and its sodium and calcium salts.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by chemical synthesis of cyclamic acid chemistry, followed where needed by conversion to sodium or calcium salts.
entries.fact_1_copy: Typically around 30–50 times sweeter than sucrose.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used as an intense sweetener and often blended with other sweeteners.
entries.fact_3_copy: The same additive number covers cyclamic acid and more soluble sodium/calcium salt forms.

entries.source_profile_definition: The same additive identity can legitimately be made from different starting materials or by different manufacturing routes. The additive code alone therefore cannot tell you one reliable origin.
entries.tile_summary: Steviol glycosides are intensely sweet compounds based on steviol, best known from the leaves of the stevia plant.
entries.expanded_summary: Steviol glycosides are intensely sweet compounds based on steviol, best known from the leaves of the stevia plant. Modern food-grade preparations can contain different purified glycosides and may be made by extraction, enzymatic conversion or fermentation-based processes depending on the specification.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Traditional preparations are extracted and purified from Stevia rebaudiana leaves; newer approved forms can use enzymes or microorganisms to convert or produce particular steviol glycosides.
entries.fact_1_copy: Stevia leaves naturally contain several steviol glycosides, including stevioside and rebaudiosides.
entries.fact_2_copy: Many individual steviol glycosides are hundreds of times sweeter than sucrose.
entries.fact_3_label: Why the source label can be nuanced
entries.fact_3_copy: The same additive family can include directly extracted and biotechnologically produced glycosides.

entries.source_profile_definition: Microorganisms such as bacteria, yeasts or fungi are grown in controlled tanks and fed sugars or other nutrients. They make the target substance as they grow. The liquid or culture is then filtered or separated, and the additive is concentrated and purified. The finished additive normally does not contain live production microbes.
entries.tile_summary: Erythritol is a four-carbon sugar alcohol that occurs naturally in small amounts in fruits and fermented foods.
entries.expanded_summary: Erythritol is a four-carbon sugar alcohol that occurs naturally in small amounts in fruits and fermented foods. Commercial erythritol is made mainly by fermentation of sugars.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by fermenting glucose with selected yeasts or fungi, then filtering, crystallising and purifying the erythritol.
entries.fact_1_copy: Found naturally at low levels in some fruits, fermented foods and beverages.
entries.fact_2_copy: About 60–80% as sweet as sucrose, with a cooling sensation.
entries.fact_3_copy: Used as a bulk sweetener and texture ingredient.
entries.evidence_copy: Higher blood erythritol levels have been associated with cardiovascular disease in observational studies. Europe's food-safety authority found that those blood levels do not necessarily measure erythritol eaten as an additive and concluded that the studies did not establish cause and effect. A better-established immediate effect is diarrhoea. The authority set an intake value of 0.5 grams per kilogram of body weight per day and estimated that some consumers could exceed it.
entries.evidence_source_1_link_label: European food-safety authority: Re-evaluation of erythritol E968 (2023)

entries.source_profile_definition: A protein that performs a specific biological job. Food enzymes may be extracted from plants or animals, or produced by microorganisms grown by fermentation. They speed up reactions such as breaking starch, protein or fat into smaller components.
entries.tile_summary: Lipases are enzymes that break down fats by splitting fatty acids from glycerol.
entries.expanded_summary: Lipases are enzymes that break down fats by splitting fatty acids from glycerol. They occur widely in living organisms and food-grade preparations are commonly made with selected microorganisms.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Commercial food lipases are usually produced by microbial fermentation and purified; some specialised enzymes may come from animal or plant sources.
entries.fact_1_copy: Hydrolyse ester bonds in fats and oils.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used in cheese flavour development, baking, fat modification and other processing.
entries.fact_3_copy: The specific enzyme preparation determines its microbial, animal or plant origin.

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with a natural material such as starch, cellulose, fat, sugar, gum or resin. It is deliberately changed using methods such as acid or alkali treatment, enzymes, heat, oxidation, or by attaching small chemical groups so it behaves differently in food — for instance to thicken better, stay stable after freezing or help oil and water stay mixed.
entries.tile_summary: Alkaline-treated starch is starch treated with alkali to change its physical and functional behaviour.
entries.expanded_summary: Alkaline-treated starch is starch treated with alkali to change its physical and functional behaviour. The starting material is ordinary food starch, but it is deliberately modified so it performs more reliably during heating, freezing, mixing or storage.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Starts with plant starch — commonly maize, potato, tapioca, wheat or another approved source — and undergoes controlled alkaline treatment, followed by washing and purification.
entries.fact_1_copy: Plant starch.
entries.fact_2_copy: Native starch can break down, thin out or retrograde under processing; modification tunes stability, viscosity, emulsification or freeze-thaw behaviour.
entries.fact_3_copy: The additive number identifies the modification, not the crop from which the starch was made.

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with a natural material such as starch, cellulose, fat, sugar, gum or resin. It is deliberately changed using methods such as acid or alkali treatment, enzymes, heat, oxidation, or by attaching small chemical groups so it behaves differently in food — for instance to thicken better, stay stable after freezing or help oil and water stay mixed.
entries.tile_summary: Phosphated distarch phosphate is cross-linked starch that also carries additional phosphate groups.
entries.expanded_summary: Phosphated distarch phosphate is cross-linked starch that also carries additional phosphate groups. The starting material is ordinary food starch, but it is deliberately modified so it performs more reliably during heating, freezing, mixing or storage.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Starts with plant starch — commonly maize, potato, tapioca, wheat or another approved source — and undergoes cross-linking plus phosphorylation, followed by washing and purification.
entries.fact_1_copy: Plant starch.
entries.fact_2_copy: Native starch can break down, thin out or retrograde under processing; modification tunes stability, viscosity, emulsification or freeze-thaw behaviour.
entries.fact_3_copy: The additive number identifies the modification, not the crop from which the starch was made.

It is deliberately changed using methods such as acid or alkali treatment, enzymes, heat, oxidation, or by attaching small chemical groups so it behaves differently in food — for instance to thicken better, stay stable after freezing or help oil and water stay mixed.
entries.tile_summary: Starch sodium octenylsuccinate is starch carrying octenylsuccinate groups in the sodium salt form.
entries.expanded_summary: Starch sodium octenylsuccinate is starch carrying octenylsuccinate groups in the sodium salt form. The starting material is ordinary food starch, but it is deliberately modified so it performs more reliably during heating, freezing, mixing or storage.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Starts with plant starch — commonly maize, potato, tapioca, wheat or another approved source — and undergoes reaction with octenylsuccinic anhydride followed by neutralisation, followed by washing and purification.
entries.fact_1_copy: Plant starch.
entries.fact_2_copy: Native starch can break down, thin out or retrograde under processing; modification tunes stability, viscosity, emulsification or freeze-thaw behaviour.
entries.fact_3_copy: The additive number identifies the modification, not the crop from which the starch was made.

It is deliberately changed using methods such as acid or alkali treatment, enzymes, heat, oxidation, or by attaching small chemical groups so it behaves differently in food — for instance to thicken better, stay stable after freezing or help oil and water stay mixed.
entries.tile_summary: Calcium lignosulphonate is a water-soluble polymeric material derived from lignin, one of the structural components of wood.
entries.expanded_summary: Calcium lignosulphonate is a water-soluble polymeric material derived from lignin, one of the structural components of wood. It is a refined by-product of sulphite wood pulping.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Recovered from sulphite pulping liquor, purified, fractionated and converted to the calcium salt form.
entries.fact_1_copy: Ultimately derived from wood lignin.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used in limited applications as a carrier, binder or dispersing material.
entries.fact_3_copy: It is not ground wood; it is a purified lignin-derived polymer fraction.

entries.source_profile_definition: Microorganisms such as bacteria, yeasts or fungi are grown in controlled tanks and fed sugars or other nutrients. They make the target substance as they grow. The liquid or culture is then filtered or separated, and the additive is concentrated and purified. The finished additive normally does not contain live production microbes.
entries.tile_summary: Sweet osmanthus ear glycolipids are natural glycolipid molecules made by the edible jelly mushroom Dacryopinax spathularia during fermentation.
entries.expanded_summary: Sweet osmanthus ear glycolipids are natural glycolipid molecules made by the edible jelly mushroom Dacryopinax spathularia during fermentation. They act as preservatives against yeasts and moulds in certain beverages.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by fermenting glucose with a non-GM strain of Dacryopinax spathularia, then removing the fungal cells, purifying the glycolipids, pasteurising and spray-drying the product.
entries.fact_1_copy: The producing organism is the edible sweet osmanthus ear / jelly mushroom Dacryopinax spathularia.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used as an antimicrobial preservative in specified beverages.
entries.fact_3_copy: FSANZ currently lists this additive by name without a numeric Schedule 8 code.
